title: [Chapitre] V. Algèbre des figures : notes manuscrites (14/06/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting: L is a finite set, and figures and multiplicities are families of nonempty subsets of L. For a family F, |F| is its support. A multifigure appears to be a figure with a largest element. 𝓜 is the poset of these objects, and page 13 discusses its connected components.

The page continues the argument that, restricted to finite families, 𝓜 is connected. The first lines should read 'on a encore connexité. En effet'.

Argument:
1. Take X ∈ 𝓜 with X ≠ {L}, and choose A ∈ X with A ≠ L.
2. X_A is the subfamily of X lying under A. X and X_A are comparable, so they lie in the same connected component, and |X_A| = A.
3. Choose x ∈ L∖A. Then Z = {B, B∪{x}, {x} | B ∈ X_A} is a multifigure: it is the cone on X_A with apex x, and its largest element is A∪{x}.
4. Z contains X_A, so they are connected. Its support is strictly larger. Iterating, every X is connected to the full figure on L, which gives connectedness.

NB (Grothendieck notes the construction has been used several times): for F, G with disjoint supports, define the join F⊠G = {A∪B | A∈F, B∈G, A and B not both ∅}. He records:
- (A∪B)° = A°∪B°.
- ∂(A∪B) = (∂A ⊠ B) ∪ (A ⊠ ∂B). This is the standard boundary formula for a join of cells.
- If F and G are multifigures with largest elements A0 and B0, then A0∪B0 is the largest element of F⊠G, so F⊠G is a multifigure.
- F⊠G contains F⊔G as a subfigure. Hence two disjoint multifigures lie in the same connected component as F⊠G.

The cone Z is the special case G = {{x}}. The final lines, partly illegible, conclude that 𝓜 is connected for finite figures and multifigures. This is consistent with p.13's remark that axiom C4 (decomposition into connected components) is then automatic. Purpose: a structural lemma in an axiomatic 'algebra of figures', a combinatorial model of cells and polyhedra with interior and boundary operators.
errors: The boundary formula is written as unions of sets, '(∂A∪B)∪(A∪∂B)'. It only makes sense read as joins, ∂A⊠B ∪ A⊠∂B; read literally it is ill-formed.
Notation is inconsistent: 'F ∈ 𝔐, G ∈ 𝔉' uses different classes for the two factors, though the subsequent statement treats both as multifigures/figures.
The connectedness argument is only sketched: the iteration up to {L} and the comparability of X with X_A are implicit. It is straightforward, though, and correct for finite L.

ideas.what: Cone on a family of subsets, used to connect any multifigure to the top object and prove connectedness of the poset 𝓜
ideas.modern_name: cone construction / contractibility via coning in the poset of complexes

ideas.what: Join F⊠G of families with disjoint supports, with interior (A∪B)° = A°∪B° and boundary ∂(A∪B) = ∂A⊠B ∪ A⊠∂B; joins of multifigures are multifigures, and F⊠G contains F⊔G
ideas.modern_name: join of simplicial complexes / face posets; Leibniz-type boundary formula for joins

deep.surprise_reason: Routine combinatorial lemmas (cone, join, connectedness) inside an unpublished axiomatic framework. Mildly interesting only as documentation of Grothendieck's 1986 'algebra of figures' project, not as new mathematics.
